## Where this chapter fits {#sec-reg-fits}

A penalty has already appeared on Day 6: the Akaike information criterion,
$\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2k$, adds a cost of 2 for every parameter the model
estimates. The cost term of the SVM on Day 8 was a second example. The trees of
Days 10 and 11 will bring two more.

Ridge and lasso regression charge the model
not for the *number* of its coefficients but for their *size*:

$$
\underbrace{\text{RSS}}_{\text{fit}} \;+\; \underbrace{\lambda \cdot \text{(size of } \beta)}_{\text{penalty}} .
$$

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Every penalised criterion in this course has the form
*fit + λ × complexity*. AIC, cost-complexity pruning and the lasso differ only
in how complexity is measured, and in whether $\lambda$ is fixed in advance or
chosen by cross-validation.
:::

Two consequences follow, and they form the main content of the chapter. First,
shrinking coefficients towards zero introduces bias on purpose, in exchange for
a reduction in variance. A biased estimator can therefore have a lower
prediction error than an unbiased one; this is the bias–variance trade-off, now
used deliberately as a method. Second, the way in which the size
of $\beta$ is measured decides whether coefficients only shrink or are set
exactly to zero. In the second case the shrinkage method is also a method for
selecting variables.

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** ISLR Chapter 6. The end of this chapter gives a reading guide with
direct links: <U+00A7>6.2 Shrinkage Methods is the core.
:::

## When least squares is not enough {#sec-ols-fails}

### Many predictors, similar predictors

Ordinary least squares (OLS) gives unbiased estimates with the smallest variance
among all linear unbiased estimators. That guarantee is narrower than it sounds.
It does not say that the variance is small, only that no other *unbiased*
estimator does better. Here, variance means sampling variance: how much the
estimate of a coefficient would change if the study were repeated with new data
from the same population. Its square root is the standard error of the
coefficient, the number that `summary()` reports next to each estimate. A large
sampling variance therefore shows up as a large standard error, and hence as a
wide confidence interval.

Two situations, both common in biological data, make this variance large.

**Many predictors relative to the number of observations.** Every coefficient
uses up a degree of freedom. When the number of predictors $p$ is not much
smaller than the number of observations $n$, little information is left per
coefficient, and the estimates vary strongly from one sample to the next. When
$p > n$, least squares has no unique solution at all.

**Correlated predictors.** When two predictors tend to rise and fall together,
the data contain much information about their *combined* effect but little
about how that effect should be divided between them. This is called
collinearity.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — **Collinearity**: two or more predictors are strongly correlated, so
that one of them can be predicted well from the others. It inflates the standard
errors of the coefficients involved, but does not bias them.
:::

In both situations the estimates remain correct *on average*, but the estimate
from a single study can lie far from the true value. Regularisation accepts a
small, deliberate error in exchange for estimates that vary much less.

### Example: biofilm formation by *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*

We use one simulated data set throughout this chapter. The simulation code is
not shown, because only its structure matters.

*Pseudomonas aeruginosa* forms biofilms in the lungs of patients with cystic
fibrosis, and clinical isolates differ strongly in how well they do so. Forty
clinical isolates were grown in flow cells for 48 hours, and for each isolate
the response is the **mean biofilm thickness (µm)**, measured by confocal
microscopy. Using the mean over replicate images avoids pseudoreplication: images
from the same flow cell are not independent. For each isolate, twelve possible
predictors were recorded:

| Variable | Meaning | Group |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `lasR` | expression of the quorum-sensing regulator *lasR* (log2 CPM) | quorum sensing |
| `las_onset` | time until the *las* quorum-sensing reporter switches on (h) | quorum sensing |
| `rhl_onset` | time until the *rhl* quorum-sensing reporter switches on (h) | quorum sensing |
| `pel` | expression of the *pel* matrix operon (log2 fold change) | quorum sensing + c-di-GMP |
| `psl` | expression of the *psl* matrix operon (log2 fold change) | c-di-GMP |
| `cdg` | intracellular c-di-GMP concentration (pmol/mg protein) | c-di-GMP |
| `twitch` | twitching motility zone (mm) | motility |
| `pilA` | expression of the type IV pilin gene *pilA* (log2 CPM) | motility |
| `swarm` | swarming motility zone (mm) | motility |
| `passages` | number of laboratory subcultures since isolation | (weakly) motility |
| `flow` | medium flow rate in the flow cell (µL/min) | independent |
| `inoculum` | inoculum density (10^7^ CFU/mL) | independent |




::: {.cell}

:::




The twelve predictors are not independent of each other. They fall into three
groups, each driven by an underlying cause that was not measured itself.
Isolates with strong **quorum sensing** have high *lasR* expression, switch on
their quorum-sensing reporters early, and express the *pel* operon more
strongly. Isolates with high **c-di-GMP signalling** have more c-di-GMP and
express *psl* and *pel* more strongly. Isolates with strong **type IV pili
activity** have high *pilA* expression and large twitching and swarming zones.
Such unmeasured causes are called latent variables.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — A **latent variable** is a variable that is not measured directly but
influences several of the variables that are measured. Because these measured
variables share the same cause, they are correlated with each other.
"Quorum-sensing activity" is latent here: it is not a column of the data, yet it
drives *lasR* expression, both reporter onset times and *pel* expression.
:::

In the simulation, only four predictors truly affect biofilm thickness: higher
*pel* expression (+0.9 µm per log2 unit, more matrix), larger twitching zones
(+0.16 µm per mm, because type IV pili help cells to form microcolonies), more
laboratory passages (−0.25 µm per passage, because isolates lose biofilm
traits when kept in the laboratory) and a higher flow rate (−0.015 µm per
µL/min, because shear detaches cells). The other eight predictors have no
effect at all; they are only correlated with the four that do. The noise
standard deviation is 0.8 µm.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — A model is **sparse** when most of its coefficients are exactly zero,
so that only a few predictors have any effect. The opposite is a **dense**
model, in which every predictor has some (often small) effect. The true model
here is sparse: 4 of 12 coefficients are non-zero.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** The data and effects are simulated for teaching. They are chosen to be
biologically plausible, but they are not results about real isolates.
:::

### Standardising the predictors

The predictors are measured in very different units (hours, mm, µL/min,
expression levels), so their coefficients cannot be compared directly. We
therefore standardise every predictor to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. A
coefficient then means: the change in biofilm thickness (µm) when that predictor
increases by one standard deviation. This is also what ridge and lasso require,
as explained in @sec-standardise.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
predictors <- setdiff(names(isolates), "thickness")
X <- scale(as.matrix(isolates[, predictors]))   # standardised predictors
y <- isolates$thickness
n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X)
c(n = n, p = p)
```

The table compares the true coefficient with the OLS estimate and its standard

1. The standard errors are large compared with the effects: between about 0.2

that a single data set of 40 isolates does not pin them down.

### How much would the estimates change in a new study?

Because the data are simulated, we can repeat the study: keep the same 40
isolates and their predictor values, draw new biofilm thicknesses 500 times,
and refit OLS each time. The spread of the estimates is the sampling variance
that the standard errors describe.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
set.seed(3)
b_rep <- t(replicate(500, coef(lm(f_true + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8) ~ X))[-1]))
colnames(b_rep) <- predictors

op <- par(mar = c(6, 4, 1, 1))
boxplot(b_rep, las = 2, col = "grey90", border = "grey40", outline = FALSE,
        ylab = "estimate (µm per SD)")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70")
points(1:p, beta_true, pch = 4, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, cex = 1.3)
par(op)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![OLS estimates of the twelve coefficients in 500 repeated studies with the same isolates. Red crosses mark the true values. The estimates are centred on the truth (unbiased), but individual studies can be far off.](09-regularisation_files/figure-html/fig-olsrepeat-1.png){#fig-olsrepeat width=768}
:::
:::




The boxes are centred on the true values, so OLS is unbiased. But they are wide,
and widest for the predictors in the correlated blocks. In a single study, the
estimate for `pel` or `twitch` can easily be only half or one and a half times
its true value, and predictors without any effect can easily receive an
estimate as large as a real effect.

### The idea of regularisation

The error of an estimate has two parts: its bias (how far it is off on
average) and its variance (how much it varies between studies). The error of a
*prediction* has a third part, the noise in the new observation itself, which no
model can remove (@sec-biasvar gives the formula). OLS has zero
bias but a large variance. Regularisation pulls all coefficients towards zero.
This introduces a small bias, because true effects are pulled down too, but it
reduces the variance much more, because the estimates can no longer swing widely
from study to study. The rest of the chapter shows how this works for ridge
regression, the lasso and the elastic net, and how the amount of pulling is
chosen.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Regularisation trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance.
When predictors are many or correlated, this gives estimates and predictions
that are, on average, closer to the truth than those of least squares.
:::

## Ridge regression {#sec-ridge}

### The penalised criterion

Least squares chooses the coefficients that minimise the residual sum of
squares,

$$
\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j x_{ij}\Big)^2 .
$$

Ridge regression adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients and chooses the
coefficients that minimise

$$
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j x_{ij}\Big)^2}_{\text{RSS: fit to the data}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2}_{\text{penalty}} ,
$$

where $\lambda \ge 0$ is the *tuning parameter* that sets how strongly large
coefficients are punished. A coefficient can only become large if it reduces the
RSS by more than it costs in penalty.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — **Ridge regression** minimises the residual sum of squares plus
$\lambda$ times the sum of the *squared* coefficients (an $\ell_2$ penalty).
:::

Four properties follow directly from the criterion.

1. If $\lambda = 0$ the penalty disappears and the ridge estimate equals the
   least squares estimate.
2. As $\lambda \to \infty$ every coefficient is driven towards zero, and the
   fitted model approaches the model with only an intercept.
3. For values in between there is a whole path of solutions, one for each value
   of $\lambda$.
4. The intercept $\beta_0$ is not penalised. Penalising it would make the fit
   depend on where the response happens to be centred, which is not a modelling
   choice anyone intends.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Ridge shrinks every coefficient but sets none of them exactly to zero.
All $p$ predictors remain in the model at every $\lambda$, so ridge regression
is a shrinkage method and not a selection method.
:::

### Standardisation is not optional {#sec-standardise}

The penalty $\sum \beta_j^2$ adds together coefficients that are measured in
different units. A predictor recorded in millimetres has a coefficient a
thousand times smaller than the same predictor recorded in metres, and is
therefore penalised a million times less. In least squares a change of units
only rescales the coefficient and leaves the fitted values unchanged; in ridge
and lasso it changes the fit.

The remedy is to standardise every predictor to a standard deviation of 1 before
penalising. **`glmnet` does this internally by default (`standardize = TRUE`) and
reports the coefficients back on the original scale**. In this chapter we have
already standardised `X` ourselves, so the coefficients are in µm per standard
deviation of each predictor and can be compared directly.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(glmnet)

grid <- 10^seq(1, -3, length.out = 100)   # decreasing, as glmnet expects

ridge_fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, family = "gaussian",
                    lambda = grid, standardize = TRUE)
```
:::




The `lambda` argument is the *grid*: the list of penalty values for which the
model is fitted, here 100 values from 10 down to 0.001 on a log scale. Each
value gives one set of coefficients, and together they form the coefficient
paths shown below. In `cv.glmnet` the same kind of grid is the set of $\lambda$
values whose cross-validated error is compared. Supplying a grid is not
required, because `glmnet` constructs a sensible one itself, but it makes the
range explicit and lets us use the same grid for ridge, lasso and elastic net. 

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** `glmnet` minimises
$\frac{1}{2n}\text{RSS} + \lambda\left[\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2 + \alpha\|\beta\|_1\right]$,
not the textbook criterion. For the lasso a textbook $\lambda$ equals $2n$ times
the `glmnet` $\lambda$; for ridge the conversion also involves the standard
deviation of $y$. Numerical values of $\lambda$ can therefore not be compared
between `glmnet` and ISLR. Only the *shape* of the results can.
:::

### The closed-form solution

Ridge regression is one of the few penalised methods with a formula. In matrix form, with centred response and standardised predictors, the criterion is

$$
\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\,\boldsymbol\beta^\top\boldsymbol\beta .
$$

Its gradient is $-2\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) + 2\lambda\boldsymbol\beta$, and setting it to zero gives

$$
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\,\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} .
$$

Compare this with the least-squares formula of Day 3: the only change is the term $\lambda\mathbf{I}$ added to $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$. That small change has two consequences.

- **The solution always exists.** The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ are $d_j^2 \ge 0$, so those of $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}$ are $d_j^2 + \lambda > 0$. The matrix is invertible even when $p > n$ or when predictors are perfectly collinear, the two cases in which least squares fails.
- **It is stable.** Least squares divides by the eigenvalues $d_j^2$, and a tiny eigenvalue, the signature of collinearity, blows the estimate up. Ridge divides by $d_j^2 + \lambda$ instead, which is never smaller than $\lambda$.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Ridge regression adds a "ridge" of size $\lambda$ to the diagonal of $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$. This is where the method gets its name.
:::

The formula can be checked against `glmnet`, provided the two definitions of $\lambda$ are matched. `glmnet` standardises with the divisor $n$ instead of $n - 1$, divides the residual sum of squares by $2n$, and rescales the response internally; a `glmnet` value $\lambda_g$ then corresponds to $\lambda = n\lambda_g/s_y$ in the formula above, with $s_y$ the standard deviation of the response.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sd_n <- function(v) sqrt(mean((v - mean(v))^2))    # standard deviation with divisor n

Xn <- scale(X, scale = apply(X, 2, sd_n))
yc <- y - mean(y)

lambda_g    <- 0.1
lambda_text <- n * lambda_g / sd_n(y)

b_formula <- solve(t(Xn) %*% Xn + lambda_text * diag(p), t(Xn) %*% yc)

fit_g    <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_g, thresh = 1e-14)
b_glmnet <- as.vector(coef(fit_g))[-1] * apply(X, 2, sd_n)

round(cbind(formula = drop(b_formula), glmnet = b_glmnet), 4)
```

### Why shrinkage helps: bias against variance {#sec-biasvar}

Suppose we use a fitted model to predict the thickness $y_0$ of a new biofilm
grown from an isolate with predictor values $x_0$. The true mean thickness for
that isolate is $f(x_0)$, and the observed value is $y_0 = f(x_0) + \varepsilon$,
where the noise $\varepsilon$ has mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2$. The prediction
$\hat f(x_0)$ depends on the data set that happened to be used for fitting, so
it differs between studies. Averaged over many possible studies, the expected
squared prediction error splits into three parts:

$$
\underbrace{E\big[(y_0 - \hat f(x_0))^2\big]}_{\text{total MSE}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\big(E[\hat f(x_0)] - f(x_0)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\big(\hat f(x_0)\big)}_{\text{variance}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible error}} .
$$

- **Squared bias**: how far the *average* prediction over many studies lies from
  the true mean. It is zero for least squares when the model contains the true
  predictors, and grows as the penalty pulls the coefficients towards zero.
- **Variance**: how much the prediction changes from one study to the next. It
  is large for least squares with many or correlated predictors, and shrinks as
  the penalty grows.
- **Irreducible error**: the noise in the new observation itself, here
  $\sigma^2 = 0.8^2 = 0.64$. No model can remove it, because it is not
  predictable from $x_0$.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Total MSE = bias² + variance + irreducible error. Regularisation
cannot touch the last term; it trades the first two against each other.
:::

Ridge estimates are biased, and the bias is not an accident but the price that
is paid on purpose. Because the data are simulated, we can measure this trade
directly. As in @fig-olsrepeat, we repeat the study 200 times with the same 40
isolates (the same `X`), draw new biofilm thicknesses each time, and decompose the
prediction error at each value of $\lambda$.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}

for (r in seq_len(R_rep)) {
  y_r <- f_true + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
  fit_r <- glmnet(X, y_r, alpha = 0, lambda = lam, standardize = TRUE)
  preds[r, , ] <- predict(fit_r, newx = X)
}

mean_pred <- apply(preds, c(2, 3), mean)   # average prediction per isolate and lambda
var_pred  <- apply(preds, c(2, 3), var)    # spread of predictions around that average

bias2 <- colMeans((mean_pred - f_true)^2)
vari  <- colMeans(var_pred)
```
:::




Only the response is redrawn in each replicate, so the variation across
replicates is pure sampling variation. The code computes the three terms of the
decomposition directly, for each $\lambda$ and averaged over the 40 isolates:
`bias2` is the squared distance between the average prediction and the true mean
`f_true`, `vari` is the variance of the predictions across the 200 studies, and
the irreducible error is the known $\sigma^2 = 0.64$. The total MSE in the figure
is their sum.

The two components move in opposite directions. The variance falls as the

### Effective degrees of freedom

The degrees-of-freedom question of Day 1 has an exact answer for ridge
regression. The cloud of observations in the space of the standardised
predictors can be described by $p$ independent directions, each with its own
amount of spread; these are the principal components of Day 4. Write
$d_j^2$ for the spread along direction $j$ (strictly, $d_j^2/(n-1)$ is the
variance along that direction; the $d_j$ are called the *singular values* of
the design matrix). Ridge regression shrinks the fit along direction $j$ by the
factor $d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda)$, where $\lambda$ is the textbook penalty.
Directions with much spread are hardly shrunk; directions with little spread —
the combinations of correlated predictors that the data hardly contain — are
shrunk strongly. Adding up these factors gives the effective degrees of freedom,

$$
\mathrm{df}(\lambda) = \sum_{j=1}^{p} \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda},
$$


which equals $p$ at $\lambda = 0$ and falls smoothly to 0 as $\lambda$ grows.
Each term lies between 0 and 1: it is 1 for a direction in the data that is
left unpenalised and 0 for a direction that is shrunk away completely.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sd_n <- function(v) sqrt(mean((v - mean(v))^2))   # glmnet standardises with 1/n

Xs <- scale(X, scale = apply(X, 2, sd_n))
d  <- svd(Xs)$d

## convert the glmnet lambda to the textbook lambda (ridge, gaussian)
lam_text <- n * lam / sd_n(y)
dfr <- sapply(lam_text, function(l) sum(d^2 / (d^2 + l)))

plot(log(lam), dfr, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, p),
     xlab = expression(log(lambda)~"(glmnet scale)"),
     ylab = "effective degrees of freedom")
abline(h = p, lty = 3); abline(v = log(lam)[i_best], lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
round(dfr[i_best], 1)
```

## The lasso {#sec-lasso}

### Replacing the squared penalty by an absolute one

The lasso uses the same residual sum of squares but a different penalty: the
sum of the *absolute* values of the coefficients. It chooses the coefficients
that minimise

$$
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j x_{ij}\Big)^2}_{\text{RSS: fit to the data}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|}_{\text{penalty}} .
$$

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — The **lasso** (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator)
minimises the residual sum of squares plus $\lambda$ times the sum of the
*absolute* coefficients (an $\ell_1$ penalty).
:::

The change from $\beta_j^2$ to $|\beta_j|$ looks small but is not. Every property
listed for ridge carries over — $\lambda = 0$ gives least squares,
$\lambda \to \infty$ gives the intercept-only model, the intercept is not
penalised — with one addition that changes the character of the method. The
lasso sets coefficients **exactly** to zero, already at finite values of
$\lambda$. It therefore performs variable selection and shrinkage in a single
step, and produces a sparse model that can be written down.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lasso_fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, family = "gaussian",
                    lambda = grid, standardize = TRUE)

plot(lasso_fit, xvar = "lambda", lwd = 1.5, label = TRUE)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Lasso coefficient paths. Coefficients reach exactly zero and stay there; the number along the top axis is the number of predictors still in the model.](09-regularisation_files/figure-html/fig-lassopath-1.png){#fig-lassopath width=672}
:::
:::




Compared with @fig-ridgepath the difference is immediate. Paths reach zero and
usually remain there, and the number along the top axis falls as the penalty
grows. The lasso moves from a model with all predictors to a model with none,
without any search over subsets of predictors. The models along the path are
not always nested: with correlated predictors one predictor can leave the model
while a correlated partner enters in its place. ISLR's version is
Figure 6.6.

### Why the absolute value produces zeros

The explanation is geometric, and it is worth working through because it also
explains what the lasso does badly. Both criteria can be written as constrained
problems: minimise the residual sum of squares subject to
$\sum_j \beta_j^2 \le s$ for ridge, or $\sum_j |\beta_j| \le s$ for the lasso.
A small budget $s$ corresponds to a large $\lambda$.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
ell <- function(centre, A, level, m = 300) {
  e  <- eigen(A)
  th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = m)
  r  <- rbind(cos(th) / sqrt(e$values[1]),
              sin(th) / sqrt(e$values[2])) * sqrt(level)
  pts <- e$vectors %*% r
  cbind(centre[1] + pts[1, ], centre[2] + pts[2, ])
}

A  <- matrix(c(1, 0.65, 0.65, 1), 2, 2)   # correlated predictors
b0 <- c(2.4, 1.0)                         # least squares estimate

rss <- function(b) drop(t(b - b0) %*% A %*% (b - b0))   # RSS up to a constant

## points on the boundary of the constraint region
boundary <- function(kind, s, m = 20000) {
  if (kind == "ridge") {
    th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = m)
    cbind(s * cos(th), s * sin(th))
  } else {
    t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)
    rbind(cbind(s * (1 - t), s * t), cbind(-s * t, s * (1 - t)),
          cbind(-s * (1 - t), -s * t), cbind(s * t, -s * (1 - t)))
  }
}

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1))

for (kind in c("lasso", "ridge")) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(-0.6, 3.2), ylim = c(-0.6, 2.4), asp = 1,
       xlab = expression(beta[1]), ylab = expression(beta[2]),
       main = kind)
  abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey70")

  s   <- if (kind == "lasso") 1.35 else 1.25
  B   <- boundary(kind, s)
  polygon(B[, 1], B[, 2], col = "#cfe0ea", border = "grey30")
  hit <- B[which.min(apply(B, 1, rss)), ]   # exact constrained solution

  lev <- as.numeric(t(hit - b0) %*% A %*% (hit - b0))
  for (f in c(0.35, 0.7, 1)) {
    e <- ell(b0, A, lev * f)
    lines(e[, 1], e[, 2], col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.4)
  }
  points(b0[1], b0[2], pch = 16, cex = 1.1)
  text(b0[1], b0[2], expression(hat(beta)^{OLS}), pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
  points(hit[1], hit[2], pch = 16, col = "firebrick", cex = 1.2)
}
par(op)
```

### The algorithm: soft-thresholding and coordinate descent

The lasso has no closed-form solution in general, because $|\beta|$ has a kink at zero and cannot be differentiated there. With a single predictor, however, the problem can be solved exactly, and the general algorithm is built from that case.

Take one standardised predictor, $\frac1n\sum_i x_i^2 = 1$, and the criterion in the scaling that `glmnet` uses,

$$
\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i\beta)^2 + \lambda\,|\beta| .
$$

Let $z = \frac1n\sum_i x_iy_i$ be the least-squares estimate. For $\beta > 0$ the derivative is $-z + \beta + \lambda$, which is zero at $\beta = z - \lambda$; this is a valid solution only if $z > \lambda$. For $\beta < 0$ the same argument gives $\beta = z + \lambda$, valid only if $z < -\lambda$. In between, neither side has a stationary point, and the minimum sits at the kink, $\beta = 0$. The three cases combine into the **soft-thresholding operator**:

$$
\hat\beta = S(z, \lambda) = \operatorname{sign}(z)\,\max\big(|z| - \lambda,\ 0\big).
$$




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
soft <- function(z, g) sign(z) * pmax(abs(z) - g, 0)

z <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 300)
plot(z, z, type = "l", lty = 3, xlab = "least-squares estimate z",
     ylab = "penalised estimate", asp = 1)
lines(z, soft(z, 1), lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
lines(z, z / (1 + 1), lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey80")
legend("topleft", c("least squares", "lasso: S(z, 1)", "ridge: z / (1 + 1)"), bty = "n",
       lwd = c(1, 2, 2), lty = c(3, 1, 1), col = c("black", "firebrick", "steelblue"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](09-regularisation_files/figure-html/soft-threshold-1.png){width=528}
:::
:::




The figure shows the two penalties side by side for $\lambda = 1$. Ridge *scales* the estimate by a constant factor, so a non-zero estimate stays non-zero. The lasso *shifts* it towards zero by $\lambda$ and sets it to exactly zero when $|z| \le \lambda$. This is the algebraic counterpart of the corner of the diamond.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — A predictor enters the lasso model only if its association with the response exceeds the threshold $\lambda$. Below that threshold its coefficient is exactly zero.
:::

With many predictors, the trick is to solve for one coefficient at a time while holding the others fixed. For coefficient $j$, compute the **partial residual**, what is left of the response after the other predictors have been accounted for, and apply the one-predictor solution to it:

$$
r_i^{(j)} = y_i - \sum_{k \ne j} x_{ik}\beta_k,
\qquad
\beta_j \leftarrow S\Big(\tfrac1n\sum_i x_{ij}\,r_i^{(j)},\ \lambda\Big).
$$

Cycling through $j = 1, \dots, p$ until nothing changes is **coordinate descent**. Because the criterion is convex, the cycle converges to the lasso solution.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lasso_cd <- function(X, y, lambda, sweeps = 200) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  b <- rep(0, ncol(X))
  r <- y - mean(y)                                # residual; the intercept is the mean
  for (s in seq_len(sweeps)) {
    for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) {
      r    <- r + X[, j] * b[j]                   # partial residual: put predictor j back
      b[j] <- soft(sum(X[, j] * r) / n, lambda)   # one-predictor solution
      r    <- r - X[, j] * b[j]                   # take the updated predictor out again
    }
  }
  b
}

lambda_l <- 0.15
b_cd  <- lasso_cd(Xn, y, lambda_l)
fit_l <- glmnet(Xn, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_l, standardize = FALSE, thresh = 1e-14)

round(cbind(coordinate_descent = b_cd, glmnet = as.vector(coef(fit_l))[-1]), 4)
```

### Which penalty is better?

Neither in general; the answer depends on the truth, not on the method. The
lasso assumes that most coefficients are zero. When that is true, it does better
than ridge, because it can exploit the sparsity. When instead every predictor
contributes a little (a dense truth), the lasso's zeros are wrong and ridge does
better.

To check this, we generate a second response for the same isolates, this time
with a small effect for every predictor, and compare the two methods on both
responses.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
y_dense    <- f_dense + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)

foldid <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = n))   # one fixed set of folds

cv_err <- function(response, alpha) {
  fit <- cv.glmnet(X, response, alpha = alpha, foldid = foldid)
  min(fit$cvm)
}
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(rbind(
  sparse_truth = c(ridge = cv_err(y, 0),       lasso = cv_err(y, 1)),
  dense_truth  = c(ridge = cv_err(y_dense, 0), lasso = cv_err(y_dense, 1))
), 2)
```

## The elastic net {#sec-enet}

The elastic net combines the two penalties. It minimises

$$
\text{RSS} \;+\; \lambda\Big[\tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2
\;+\; \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|\Big],
$$

where the mixing parameter $\alpha$ lies between 0 and 1: $\alpha = 0$ gives
ridge regression, $\alpha = 1$ the lasso, and values in between a mixture. This
is the criterion that `glmnet` uses for all three methods, which is why its
`alpha` argument selects the method.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — The **elastic net** penalises a weighted mixture of the squared and
the absolute coefficients; $\alpha$ sets the mix, $\lambda$ the overall
strength.
:::

The elastic net exists because the weaknesses of the two methods are
complementary. Ridge handles correlated predictors well but never selects; the
lasso selects but handles correlated predictors badly. Mixing the penalties
keeps the zeros of the lasso, while correlated predictors tend to enter or leave
the model together and share the coefficient between them, rather than one of
them taking all of it. This is called the *grouping* effect.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
enet_fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5, lambda = grid, standardize = TRUE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4, 5, 1))
plot(ridge_fit, xvar = "lambda", lwd = 1.1); title("ridge (alpha = 0)", line = 3.2)
plot(enet_fit,  xvar = "lambda", lwd = 1.1); title("elastic net (alpha = 0.5)", line = 3.2)
plot(lasso_fit, xvar = "lambda", lwd = 1.1); title("lasso (alpha = 1)", line = 3.2)
par(op)
```

:::
:::




Compare the three panels at the same position on the $x$-axis. The number of
remaining coefficients falls from left to right, and the elastic net lies

it spreads a signal over a group of correlated predictors instead of assigning

$\alpha$ is a second tuning parameter. In principle $\alpha$ and $\lambda$
should be chosen together; in practice a small set of three or four values of
$\alpha$, each with its own cross-validated $\lambda$ on the same folds, is
sufficient.

## Choosing $\lambda$ {#sec-lambda}

### Cross-validation, again

Nothing in the criterion determines $\lambda$. A larger $\lambda$ never fits the
training data better, so the training error keeps decreasing as $\lambda$
decreases and is useless for choosing it. The quantity that has a minimum is the
error on new data, and that is estimated by cross-validation.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(253)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, type.measure = "mse",
                      nfolds = 10, standardize = TRUE)

plot(cv_lasso)
```

everything away, a minimum, and a rise as the penalty weakens towards the
overfitted least squares solution. The top axis counts non-zero coefficients, so
the plot reports error and model size at the same time. ISLR's equivalent is
Figure 6.13.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
  lambda_1se = cv_lasso$lambda.1se,
  nz_min     = cv_lasso$nzero[cv_lasso$index["min", 1]],
  nz_1se     = cv_lasso$nzero[cv_lasso$index["1se", 1]])
```

Two values are returned. `lambda.min` minimises the cross-validated error.
`lambda.1se` is the largest $\lambda$ whose error lies within one standard error
of that minimum. This is the **one-standard-error rule** of Day 7, applied here for the same reason: a difference
smaller than the uncertainty of the estimates is not evidence, and when the data
cannot distinguish two models, we prefer the simpler one.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — `lambda.1se` usually gives a clearly smaller model at almost no cost in

default; for pure prediction, `lambda.min`.

### Penalised coefficients are not estimates of the true effects {#sec-shrunken}

The selected coefficients should not be read as estimates of the true effect
sizes. The penalty pulls every coefficient towards zero, so a penalised
coefficient is usually *smaller* in absolute value than the true coefficient —
and the stronger the penalty, the stronger this shrinkage. In addition, when a
signal is shared by correlated predictors, it may be divided over several of
them. We can check both effects here, because the truth is known.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cv_ridge <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, foldid = foldid)
cv_las_f <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, foldid = foldid)

round(data.frame(
  true      = beta_true,
  ols       = unname(coef(ols)[-1]),
  ridge_1se = as.vector(coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1],
  lasso_min = as.vector(coef(cv_las_f, s = "lambda.min"))[-1],
  lasso_1se = as.vector(coef(cv_las_f, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1],
  row.names = predictors
), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

Compare the columns row by row.

- **OLS** gives every predictor a coefficient. Two true effects (`passages`,
  `flow`) are overestimated, and several predictors without effect (`psl`,
  `cdg`, `inoculum`) get sizeable coefficients.
- **Lasso** sets most predictors without effect exactly to zero. The true
  effects keep the right sign but are *smaller* than the truth, and smaller at
  `lambda.1se` than at `lambda.min`, because the penalty is larger there.
  `swarm` is kept with a small coefficient: it is correlated with `twitch` and
  takes over a little of its effect.
- **Ridge** at `lambda.1se` keeps all twelve predictors but shrinks them all
  strongly, the true effects included, to about 0.1 µm.

In every penalised column, the size of a coefficient reflects the penalty as
much as the true effect.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — A penalised coefficient answers the question "what coefficient gives
the best predictions under this penalty?", not "what is the true effect of this
predictor?". Its size depends on $\lambda$ and on which correlated predictors
happened to be kept.
:::

It is tempting to refit an ordinary linear model on the selected predictors and
report the resulting table. This should be avoided. The predictors in that table
were chosen *because* they appeared strongly associated with the response in
this sample. The $p$-values are computed as if the predictors had been chosen in
advance, so they are too small, and the confidence intervals too narrow.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** This is the most consequential error in applied use of the lasso. The
selection step is part of the analysis and must be accounted for. Valid
post-selection inference exists — the `selectiveInference` package implements
it — but it is not obtained by refitting with `lm` and reading off the stars.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** This is the double dipping of Day 2 (Exercise 2.1) in another guise: the data chose the variables, and the same data are then asked to test them.
:::

An honest summary of a lasso analysis is a prediction error estimated by
cross-validation, together with the selected set of predictors, described as a
set. If the aim is a statement about the effect of one particular predictor, a
regularised model is the wrong tool; a study designed with that predictor
specified in advance is the right one.

## Practical matters {#sec-practice}

### Building the design matrix

`glmnet` takes a numeric matrix, not a formula, so factors must be converted to
dummy variables first.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Xmat <- model.matrix(~ ., data = predictors)[, -1]
```
:::




The `[, -1]` removes the intercept column, which `glmnet` adds itself and must
not penalise. A factor with $k$ levels becomes $k-1$ dummy columns, each
penalised separately. The penalty may therefore keep some levels of a factor and
drop others, a result that is often awkward to interpret. The `grpreg` package
implements a group lasso that treats all dummy columns of a factor as one unit.

### Interactions are not discovered

Ridge and lasso are linear models. They do not search for interactions, and
unlike a tree they will not find one by accident. If an interaction is expected,
it must be written into the design matrix.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Xmat_int <- model.matrix(~ .^2, data = predictors)[, -1]
```
:::




This is the sharpest contrast with the tree-based methods of Days 10 and 11. A random forest finds
interactions automatically but does not report what they are; a penalised
regression requires them to be specified, and then reports their coefficients.

### Other response distributions

The `family` argument carries the penalised criterion over to generalised linear
models, with the deviance in place of the residual sum of squares:
`family = "binomial"` for logistic regression, `"multinomial"` for more than two
categories, `"poisson"` for counts, and `"cox"` for survival times.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** `glmnet` has no dispersion parameter. With `family = "poisson"` it fits
the Poisson mean structure but does not model overdispersion, so predictions are
usable while the deviance-based error is not comparable to that of a negative
binomial model.
:::


## Regression on a few derived variables {#sec-pcr}

Penalisation is not the only answer to having too many correlated predictors.
The alternative is to replace the predictors by a small number of new variables,
each a weighted combination of all the original ones, and to regress the
response on those. The construction of the new variables, principal component analysis (PCA), was the subject of Day 4.

### Principal components regression

In the isolate data, nine of the twelve predictors are driven by three latent
variables. PCA finds new variables, called principal components, that capture
as much as possible of the variation among the predictors: the first component
is the weighted combination of predictors with the largest variance, the second
the combination with the next-largest variance that is uncorrelated with the
first, and so on. When a few latent variables drive many measured variables, the
first few components capture most of the variation.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — **Principal components regression (PCR)** computes the first $M$
principal components of the predictors and regresses the response on those $M$
components by ordinary least squares.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(pls)

iso_df <- data.frame(thickness = y, X)

set.seed(31)
pcr_fit <- pcr(thickness ~ ., data = iso_df, scale = TRUE, validation = "CV")

validationplot(pcr_fit, val.type = "MSEP",
               xlab = "number of components", main = "")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-validated error of principal components regression against the number of components.](09-regularisation_files/figure-html/pcr-fit-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::




The curve shows the cross-validated error for 0 to 12 components. With all 12
components, PCR is identical to least squares; with fewer, it uses only the
directions in which the predictors vary most. The curve is not smooth: the
error hardly falls for the first five components and drops only at the sixth.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ncomp_best <- selectNcomp(pcr_fit, method = "onesigma", plot = FALSE)
ncomp_best
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 1
```


:::
:::




`selectNcomp` with `method = "onesigma"` applies the one-standard-error rule
once more: it returns the smallest number of components whose error lies within
one standard error of the minimum, here 1. The cross-validated
error of that model
(1.37) is much worse than
that of the lasso (0.9). PCR does badly on these
data, and the next section explains why.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** PCR is not a variable-selection method. Every component is a combination
of all twelve predictors, so no predictor is ever dropped; the model is small in
components but uses every original variable.
:::

### Why unsupervised directions can fail

PCR chooses its components by looking only at `X`, never at the response. The
directions that explain most of the variation among the predictors need not be
the ones that predict the response: a high-variance direction may be irrelevant,
and a low-variance direction may carry all the signal. PCR cannot detect this.

That is what happens here. The first components describe the three correlated
blocks (quorum sensing, c-di-GMP, motility), because that is where most of the
variation among the predictors lies. But two of the four true effects,
`passages` and `flow`, are hardly correlated with anything else, so they only
appear in later
components with little variance. PCR needs many components before it reaches
them. Variance is not the same as relevance.

Ridge regression can be seen as a smooth version of PCR. Instead of keeping the
first $M$ components completely and discarding the rest, ridge shrinks every
component by the factor $d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda)$ — strongly for low-variance
directions and weakly for high-variance ones. This is the same expression that
appeared in the effective degrees of freedom, and it explains why ridge and PCR
usually give similar results. Figure 6.19 compares them
directly.

### Partial least squares

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — **Partial least squares (PLS)** constructs new variables that have high
variance *and* are correlated with the response, so that the response guides the
choice of directions.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(32)
pls_fit <- plsr(thickness ~ ., data = iso_df, scale = TRUE, validation = "CV")

validationplot(pls_fit, val.type = "MSEP",
               xlab = "number of components", main = "")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](09-regularisation_files/figure-html/pls-fit-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
selectNcomp(pls_fit, method = "onesigma", plot = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 1
```


:::
:::




PLS typically needs fewer components than PCR, because each direction is chosen
for its relation with the response and not only for its variance. Here its
error is lowest with three components
(1), clearly better than PCR
with the same number of components, although still not as good as the lasso.
Using the response to choose the directions reduces bias but adds variance,
since the response is now used twice.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** Because PLS uses the response to construct its components, the
construction must be repeated *inside* every cross-validation fold. `plsr` with
`validation = "CV"` does this; computing the components once on the full data
and then cross-validating only the regression gives an optimistic error.
:::

PLS is standard practice in chemometrics and spectroscopy, where the number of
correlated predictors (for example, reflectance at hundreds of wavelengths) is
often far larger than the number of samples.

## A common view {#sec-unified}

Six methods have now been applied to the same problem, and their differences
come down to a few choices.

| Method | Penalty or restriction | Sets coefficients to zero | Handles correlated predictors | Tuning |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Least squares | none | no | badly | none |
| Ridge | $\lambda\sum\beta_j^2$ | no | well | $\lambda$ |
| Lasso | $\lambda\sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert$ | yes | badly | $\lambda$ |
| Elastic net | mixture | yes | well | $\lambda, \alpha$ |
| PCR | first $M$ components | no | well | $M$ |
| PLS | first $M$ supervised components | no | well | $M$ |

One further reading of the same penalties is worth knowing.

**The Bayesian reading.** Ridge regression gives the most probable coefficients
(the posterior mode) when each coefficient has a normal prior distribution with
mean 0. The lasso gives the posterior mode when each coefficient has a Laplace
(double-exponential) prior, which has a sharp peak at zero — the probabilistic
counterpart of the corner of the diamond. In both cases $\lambda$ expresses how
large the coefficients were expected to be before the data were seen.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — A penalty acts as a prior, and cross-validation is a way of choosing
that prior from the data. This is why the same device can be described either as
regularisation or as shrinkage towards a population mean.
:::

## Where this leads {#sec-next}

Every method covered since the resampling chapter chooses a position on the same scale. At one end is a model flexible enough to reproduce the training data exactly and useless on anything else; at the other, a model so constrained that it ignores the data. KNN chooses its position through $k$, the SVM through its cost, and penalised regression through $\lambda$. In every case the position is chosen by cross-validation, because counting parameters, as on Day 1, no longer measures what it needs to measure.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Day 1 asked what the data can resolve, and answered by counting parameters. The answer now is to measure the same thing empirically, by withholding data and checking the predictions.
:::

None of these methods provides straightforward inference. They produce no coefficient with a trustworthy standard error, no valid $p$-value and no interpretable effect size. They are tools for predicting an outcome. Knowing which question is being asked is the basis for choosing between them.

The next two days make the same trade with a very different kind of model: the tree.
